lessons.title: Financial records and statements
lessons.html:
The farm as a business

A dairy can have excellent cows and still fail financially. Farm business management means planning, organising and controlling resources so the farm is profitable, liquid and solvent over the long term.

Three key financial statements

StatementShowsKey question
Income statementIncome minus expenses over a periodIs the farm profitable?
Balance sheetAssets, liabilities and owner's equity at a point in timeIs the farm solvent; what is it worth?
Cash flow statementCash in and out over timeCan the farm pay its bills when they fall due?

Income and costs on a dairy

  • Income: milk sales (the main item), cull cow sales, bull calf and heifer sales, and sometimes crop or silage sales.
  • Variable (direct) costs: feed, fertiliser and seed for pasture, animal health, semen, parlour consumables, electricity for milking and cooling, fuel.
  • Fixed (overhead) costs: permanent labour, insurance, depreciation, interest, rates, administration.

Gross margin

The gross margin of the dairy enterprise is gross income minus variable costs. It shows how much the enterprise contributes towards fixed costs and profit, and is used to compare enterprises or years.

Example per month: milk income R1 200 000 plus cull sales R60 000 equals R1 260 000. Variable costs R820 000. Gross margin = R440 000. If fixed costs are R310 000, net farm income before tax is R130 000.

Good record keeping

Accurate financial records are needed for decisions, loans, tax and compliance. Keep all invoices, statements and payroll records, reconcile bank accounts monthly, and use a farm accounting package or bookkeeper. Payroll must comply with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and tax and UIF obligations.

lessons.title: Budgeting and financial analysis
lessons.html:
Budgets as planning tools

  • Enterprise budget: expected income and variable costs for the dairy enterprise, giving a projected gross margin.
  • Whole-farm budget: all enterprises plus fixed costs, giving projected net farm income.
  • Cash flow budget: month-by-month cash in and out, showing when overdraft is needed.
  • Partial budget: evaluates a single change, such as buying a mixer wagon or increasing cow numbers, by listing additional income, reduced costs, additional costs and lost income.
  • Capital budget: evaluates larger investments using payback period, net present value or return on investment.

Partial budget example

Proposal: install fans and sprinklers in the feed pad to reduce heat stress. Cost R350 000, depreciated over 10 years (R35 000 per year), plus R15 000 per year electricity and maintenance. Expected gain: 1 litre more per cow per day for 120 hot days on 400 cows = 48 000 litres at a margin of R4.00 = R192 000 per year. Net benefit = R192 000 − R35 000 − R15 000 = R142 000 per year, before interest. The manager should also test what happens if the yield gain is only half.

Financial ratios

RatioMeasures
Current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities)Liquidity
Debt ratio (total liabilities ÷ total assets)Solvency
Return on assetsProfitability of capital invested
Feed cost per litre, margin over feed per litreDairy operational efficiency

Sensitivity analysis

Milk price and feed price are the biggest drivers of dairy profit. Test budgets at lower milk prices and higher feed prices to understand the farm's break-even point and risk exposure.

lessons.title: Managing resources, risk and the market
lessons.html:
Managing the factors of production

  • Land: owned or leased; productivity depends on soils, water and conservation. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 applies.
  • Labour: recruitment, training, retention and compliance with the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995, the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998.
  • Capital: livestock, machinery, buildings, working capital. Finance through own funds, bank loans, asset finance or Land Bank, considering interest cost and repayment capacity.
  • Management: the skill to combine the other resources effectively.

Business risk

Risk typeExamplesResponses
ProductionDrought, diseaseFeed reserves, biosecurity, insurance
MarketMilk price dropSupply contracts, cost control, diversification
FinancialRising interest rates, high debtConservative gearing, cash reserves
LegalLabour disputes, environmental non-complianceCompliance systems, advice
HumanLoss of key staff, injurySuccession planning, safety, cross-training

Marketing milk

Most producers sell under a supply agreement with a processor. Understand the contract: price formula, quality and component payments, volume commitments, penalties, payment terms and notice periods. Compare offers from buyers where possible. Value-adding through on-farm processing can raise margins but brings food safety compliance under the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 and new marketing risks.

Business planning

A business plan states the vision, goals, market, production plan, financial projections and risks. It guides decisions and is required by lenders. Review it yearly.

Key points

  • Use the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement together.
  • Gross margin is income minus variable costs.
  • Use partial budgets for single decisions and test sensitivity.
  • Monitor liquidity, solvency and profitability ratios.
  • Understand milk contracts and manage production, market, financial, legal and human risk.
